claim: GREM1 was undetectable in healthy human liver by RNAscope in situ hybridisation.
source: GREM1 was undetectable in healthy human liver by RNAscope in situ hybridisation (ISH) but staining increased in fibrotic MASH liver, localising to the fibrotic septa (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Directly stated observation from RNAscope ISH experiments on healthy human liver tissue.

claim: GREM1 staining increased in fibrotic MASH liver.
source: GREM1 was undetectable in healthy human liver by RNAscope in situ hybridisation (ISH) but staining increased in fibrotic MASH liver, localising to the fibrotic septa (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Directly stated observation from RNAscope ISH experiments comparing healthy and fibrotic MASH liver.

claim: GREM1 localises to the fibrotic septa in MASH liver.
source: GREM1 was undetectable in healthy human liver by RNAscope in situ hybridisation (ISH) but staining increased in fibrotic MASH liver, localising to the fibrotic septa (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Directly stated observation from RNAscope ISH experiments showing spatial localization.

claim: There was a 4.8- to 9.8-fold increase in GREM1 mRNA expression in MASH, ALD, PBC, and PSC liver tissues when compared to donor livers.
source: By RTqPCR of human explant livers of different aetiologies (all fibrosis stage F4), we observed a 4.8- to 9.8-fold increase in GREM1 mRNA expression in MASH, ALD, PBC, and PSC liver tissues when compared to donor livers (n=13–15 each, Figure 1C).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from RTqPCR experiments on human liver tissues.

claim: GREM1 expression does not correlate with the histological stage of fibrosis in MASLD patients.
source: Notably though, when analysing publicly available bulk RNA-sequencing data from a total of 352 patients with MASLD (n=58 E-MTAB-9815, n=78 GSE130970, n=216 GSE135251), capturing the whole spectrum of MASLD and MASH, we found no correlation of GREM1 expression with the histological stage of fibrosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Analysis of publicly available RNA-sequencing datasets from 352 MASLD patients.

claim: GREM1 mRNA-positive cells stained positive for THY1 and COL3A1 in RNAscope ISH.
source: GREM1 mRNA-positive cells also stained positive for THY1 and COL3A1 in RNAscope ISH (Figure 1D), indicating that myofibroblasts in the fibrotic area were the major cell type expressing Gremlin-1 in human MASH.
evidence: Direct observation from co-staining experiments using RNAscope ISH.

claim: Myofibroblasts in the fibrotic area are the major cell type expressing Gremlin-1 in human MASH.
source: GREM1 mRNA-positive cells also stained positive for THY1 and COL3A1 in RNAscope ISH (Figure 1D), indicating that myofibroblasts in the fibrotic area were the major cell type expressing Gremlin-1 in human MASH.
evidence: Inference based on co-localization of GREM1 with myofibroblast markers THY1 and COL3A1.

claim: GREM1 mRNA expression was highest in primary human hepatic stellate cells (HHSC) and myofibroblasts compared to biliary epithelial and sinusoidal endothelial cells.
source: This was corroborated by findings from RTqPCR on cultured hepatic cells where GREM1 mRNA expression was highest in primary human hepatic stellate cells (HHSC) and myofibroblasts as compared to absent or low expression in biliary epithelial and sinusoidal endothelial cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from RTqPCR experiments on different cultured hepatic cell types.

claim: Only a small proportion of THY1/COL3A1+ cells expressed GREM1.
source: However, only a small proportion of THY1/COL3A1+ cells expressed GREM1, with expression being highly variable across and within each specimen.
evidence: Observation from RNAscope ISH experiments showing heterogeneous expression patterns.

claim: GREM1 expression is highly variable across and within each specimen.
source: However, only a small proportion of THY1/COL3A1+ cells expressed GREM1, with expression being highly variable across and within each specimen.
evidence: Observation from RNAscope ISH experiments showing heterogeneous expression patterns.

claim: Integrated analyses of two publicly available single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets showed very low expression levels of Gremlin-1 across cell types.
source: In agreement, integrated analyses of two publicly available single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-sequencing) datasets overall showed very low expression levels of Gremlin-1 across cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C), but slightly higher expression in THY1 and COL3A1-expressing myofibroblast populations and smooth muscle cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: Analysis of publicly available scRNA-sequencing datasets (GSE136103 and GSE192742).

claim: Gremlin-1 shows slightly higher expression in THY1 and COL3A1-expressing myofibroblast populations and smooth muscle cells.
source: In agreement, integrated analyses of two publicly available single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-sequencing) datasets overall showed very low expression levels of Gremlin-1 across cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C), but slightly higher expression in THY1 and COL3A1-expressing myofibroblast populations and smooth muscle cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: Analysis of publicly available scRNA-sequencing datasets showing cell-type specific expression patterns.

claim: Grem1 ISH staining was consistently increased in livers of rats fed a choline-deficient, L-amino acid defined high-fat diet (CDAA-HFD) for 12 weeks.
source: However, Grem1 ISH staining was consistently increased in livers of rats fed a choline-deficient, L-amino acid defined high-fat diet (CDAA-HFD) for 12 weeks.
evidence: Direct observation from ISH experiments on rat liver tissue from CDAA-HFD model.

claim: Grem1 expression in rat livers mainly localised to the periportal and fibrotic areas.
source: Like our observations in human MASH liver tissue, Grem1 expression in rat livers mainly localised to the periportal and fibrotic areas (Figure 1F).
evidence: Direct observation from ISH experiments showing spatial localization in rat liver.

claim: There was no Gremlin-1 protein signal in healthy rat liver by immunohistochemistry.
source: We observed a similar pattern when staining for Gremlin-1 protein by immunohistochemistry (IHC) in rat livers, where there was no signal in healthy rat liver and at most a weak signal in the portal and fibrotic areas in the CDAA-HFD model (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Direct observation from IHC experiments on healthy rat liver tissue.

claim: There was at most a weak Gremlin-1 protein signal in the portal and fibrotic areas in the CDAA-HFD rat model.
source: We observed a similar pattern when staining for Gremlin-1 protein by immunohistochemistry (IHC) in rat livers, where there was no signal in healthy rat liver and at most a weak signal in the portal and fibrotic areas in the CDAA-HFD model (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Direct observation from IHC experiments on CDAA-HFD rat liver tissue.

claim: Increased circulating Gremlin-1 protein has been described in patients with type 2 diabetes and in MASH.
source: Increased circulating Gremlin-1 protein has been described in patients with type 2 diabetes and in MASH, and has been linked to higher MASH disease severity (Hedjazifar et al., 2020).
evidence: Reference to published literature by Hedjazifar et al., 2020.

claim: Circulating Gremlin-1 has been linked to higher MASH disease severity.
source: Increased circulating Gremlin-1 protein has been described in patients with type 2 diabetes and in MASH, and has been linked to higher MASH disease severity (Hedjazifar et al., 2020).
evidence: Reference to published literature by Hedjazifar et al., 2020.

claim: The authors were unable to detect circulating Gremlin-1 in plasma or serum in a cohort of healthy subjects and MASLD patients with different stages of fibrosis.
source: However, despite high sensitivity, we were unable to detect circulating Gremlin-1 in plasma or serum in a cohort of healthy subjects and MASLD patients with different stages of fibrosis (Figure 2A and B, clinical characteristics see Table 1).
evidence: Direct observation from LOCI assay experiments on human plasma and serum samples.

claim: No signal for Gremlin-1 was found using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry.
source: Similarly, we found no signal for Gremlin-1 using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS).
evidence: Direct observation from LC-MS experiments on human samples.

claim: Dimeric Gremlin-1 forms dimers and trimers in complex with heparin under cell- and matrix-free conditions.
source: Using size exclusion chromatography, we observed that dimeric Gremlin-1 forms dimers and trimers in complex with heparin under cell- and matrix-free conditions (Figure 2C), suggesting that Gremlin-1 might be retained on cell surfaces and extracellular matrix and thus not enter the systemic circulation.
evidence: Direct observation from size exclusion chromatography experiments.

claim: Gremlin-1 might be retained on cell surfaces and extracellular matrix and thus not enter the systemic circulation.
source: Using size exclusion chromatography, we observed that dimeric Gremlin-1 forms dimers and trimers in complex with heparin under cell- and matrix-free conditions (Figure 2C), suggesting that Gremlin-1 might be retained on cell surfaces and extracellular matrix and thus not enter the systemic circulation.
evidence: Inference based on size exclusion chromatography results showing Gremlin-1/heparin complex formation.

claim: The binding affinity of Gremlin-1 to heparin was in the low nanomolar range.
source: Furthermore, the binding affinity of Gremlin-1 to heparin was in the low nanomolar range (Figure 3E), suggesting a strong localisation towards extracellular matrix proteoglycans.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from fluorescence polarisation assay experiments.

claim: The low nanomolar binding affinity of Gremlin-1 to heparin suggests a strong localisation towards extracellular matrix proteoglycans.
source: Furthermore, the binding affinity of Gremlin-1 to heparin was in the low nanomolar range (Figure 3E), suggesting a strong localisation towards extracellular matrix proteoglycans.
evidence: Inference based on measured binding affinity data.

claim: Generated antibodies were highly effective in blocking recombinant human Gremlin-1 from binding BMP4 in a Gremlin/BMP4 inhibition ELISA with IC50=2.7–3.1 × 10–9 M.
source: Generated antibodies were highly effective in blocking recombinant human Gremlin-1 from binding BMP4 in a Gremlin/BMP4 inhibition enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) (Figure 3A, IC50=2.7–3.1 × 10–9 M) as well as in a BRE-Luc RGA BMP reporter assay (Figure 3B, EC50=1.27–1.36 × 10–8 M) with IC50/EC50 values being the lowest possible that can be reached given the amount of Gremlin-1 used in the assays.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from ELISA experiments testing antibody efficacy.

claim: Generated antibodies were highly effective in a BRE-Luc RGA BMP reporter assay with EC50=1.27–1.36 × 10–8 M.
source: Generated antibodies were highly effective in blocking recombinant human Gremlin-1 from binding BMP4 in a Gremlin/BMP4 inhibition enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) (Figure 3A, IC50=2.7–3.1 × 10–9 M) as well as in a BRE-Luc RGA BMP reporter assay (Figure 3B, EC50=1.27–1.36 × 10–8 M) with IC50/EC50 values being the lowest possible that can be reached given the amount of Gremlin-1 used in the assays.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from BRE-Luc reporter assay experiments testing antibody efficacy.

claim: Treatment of LX-2 cells with BMP4 increased SMAD1 phosphorylation.
source: Treatment of LX-2 cells with BMP4 also increased SMAD1 phosphorylation, which was prevented by the addition of Gremlin-1 protein (Figure 3C), and anti-Gremlin-1 antibodies, but not isotype control, effectively restored SMAD1 phosphorylation in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3C, KD = 2.04–2.96 × 10–9 M).
evidence: Direct observation from cell culture experiments measuring SMAD1 phosphorylation.

claim: Addition of Gremlin-1 protein prevented BMP4-induced SMAD1 phosphorylation in LX-2 cells.
source: Treatment of LX-2 cells with BMP4 also increased SMAD1 phosphorylation, which was prevented by the addition of Gremlin-1 protein (Figure 3C), and anti-Gremlin-1 antibodies, but not isotype control, effectively restored SMAD1 phosphorylation in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3C, KD = 2.04–2.96 × 10–9 M).
evidence: Direct observation from cell culture experiments measuring SMAD1 phosphorylation.

claim: Anti-Gremlin-1 antibodies, but not isotype control, effectively restored SMAD1 phosphorylation in a dose-dependent manner with KD = 2.04–2.96 × 10–9 M.
source: Treatment of LX-2 cells with BMP4 also increased SMAD1 phosphorylation, which was prevented by the addition of Gremlin-1 protein (Figure 3C), and anti-Gremlin-1 antibodies, but not isotype control, effectively restored SMAD1 phosphorylation in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3C, KD = 2.04–2.96 × 10–9 M).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from cell culture experiments testing antibody efficacy on SMAD1 phosphorylation.

claim: The 0032:ND/0568:ND antibody formed complexes with Gremlin-1 dimers in a 2:2 ratio.
source: Antibodies differed in their binding stoichiometries; the 0032:ND/0568:ND antibody formed complexes with Gremlin-1 dimers in a 2:2 ratio, whilst the 0030:HD compound bound Gremlin-1 predominantly in a 1:1 ratio (Figure 3D).
evidence: Direct observation from size exclusion chromatography experiments.

claim: The 0030:HD compound bound Gremlin-1 predominantly in a 1:1 ratio.
source: Antibodies differed in their binding stoichiometries; the 0032:ND/0568:ND antibody formed complexes with Gremlin-1 dimers in a 2:2 ratio, whilst the 0030:HD compound bound Gremlin-1 predominantly in a 1:1 ratio (Figure 3D).
evidence: Direct observation from size exclusion chromatography experiments.

claim: Gremlin-1 bound to heparin with high affinity (KD [Grem1 alone]=13 nM).
source: Using a fluorescence polarisation assay, we found that Gremlin-1 bound to heparin with high affinity (Figure 3E, KD [Grem1 alone]=13 nM), confirming our chromatography findings.
evidence: Quantitative measurement from fluorescence polarisation assay experiments.

claim: The 0032:ND compound did not affect heparin binding of Gremlin-1.
source: Whilst the 0032:ND compound did not affect heparin binding of Gremlin-1, the 0030:HD heparin-displacing antibody reduced the affinity by a factor of 10 (KD [0032:ND- Gremlin-1]=18 nM vs KD [0030:HD- Gremlin-1]=99 nM, respectively, Figure 3E).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from fluorescence polarisation assay experiments.

claim: The 0030:HD heparin-displacing antibody reduced the affinity of Gremlin-1 for heparin by a factor of 10 (KD [0032:ND- Gremlin-1]=18 nM vs KD [0030:HD- Gremlin-1]=99 nM).
source: Whilst the 0032:ND compound did not affect heparin binding of Gremlin-1, the 0030:HD heparin-displacing antibody reduced the affinity by a factor of 10 (KD [0032:ND- Gremlin-1]=18 nM vs KD [0030:HD- Gremlin-1]=99 nM, respectively, Figure 3E).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from fluorescence polarisation assay experiments.

claim: Atto-532-conjugated Gremlin-1 bound to the cell surface of LX-2 cells.
source: In line with these results, Atto-532-conjugated Gremlin-1 bound to the cell surface of LX-2 cells which was prevented by the heparin-displacing 0030:HD but not the 0032:ND or isotype control antibody (Figure 3F).
evidence: Direct observation from confocal microscopy experiments on LX-2 cells.

claim: The heparin-displacing 0030:HD antibody prevented Atto-532-conjugated Gremlin-1 from binding to the cell surface of LX-2 cells.
source: In line with these results, Atto-532-conjugated Gremlin-1 bound to the cell surface of LX-2 cells which was prevented by the heparin-displacing 0030:HD but not the 0032:ND or isotype control antibody (Figure 3F).
evidence: Direct observation from confocal microscopy experiments on LX-2 cells.

claim: The 0032:ND antibody did not prevent Atto-532-conjugated Gremlin-1 from binding to the cell surface of LX-2 cells.
source: In line with these results, Atto-532-conjugated Gremlin-1 bound to the cell surface of LX-2 cells which was prevented by the heparin-displacing 0030:HD but not the 0032:ND or isotype control antibody (Figure 3F).
evidence: Direct observation from confocal microscopy experiments on LX-2 cells.

claim: The 0030:HD antibody forms 1:1 complexes with free Gremlin-1 not involving heparin.
source: Size exclusion chromatography on mixtures of Gremlin-1, heparin, and anti-Gremlin-1 antibodies revealed that the 0030:HD antibody forms 1:1 complexes with free Gremlin-1 not involving heparin, while the 0032:ND antibody captures heparin-bound Gremlin-1, leading to the formation of higher-order complexes that were insoluble and precipitated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct observation from size exclusion chromatography experiments.

claim: The 0032:ND antibody captures heparin-bound Gremlin-1, leading to the formation of higher-order complexes that were insoluble and precipitated.
source: Size exclusion chromatography on mixtures of Gremlin-1, heparin, and anti-Gremlin-1 antibodies revealed that the 0030:HD antibody forms 1:1 complexes with free Gremlin-1 not involving heparin, while the 0032:ND antibody captures heparin-bound Gremlin-1, leading to the formation of higher-order complexes that were insoluble and precipitated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct observation from size exclusion chromatography experiments.

claim: Anti-Gremlin-1 blockade did not change the expression of COL1A1, ACTA2, or TIMP1 in primary HHSC or myofibroblasts.
source: However, anti-Gremlin-1 blockade did not change the expression of COL1A1, ACTA2, or TIMP1 either without or with TGFβ1 treatment, when compared to isotype control in primary HHSC or myofibroblasts (p>0.05, Figure 4A and B, respectively).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from qPCR experiments on primary human cells.

claim: Lentiviral overexpression increased the expression of GREM1 by a factor of 177 after sorting for GFP positivity in LX-2.
source: Overexpression increased the expression of GREM1 by a factor of 177 after sorting for GFP positivity in LX-2 (p<0.001, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) and by a factor of 6.3 in unsorted HHSC (p=0.0204, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from qPCR experiments on lentivirally transduced cells.

claim: Lentiviral overexpression increased the expression of GREM1 by a factor of 6.3 in unsorted HHSC.
source: Overexpression increased the expression of GREM1 by a factor of 177 after sorting for GFP positivity in LX-2 (p<0.001, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) and by a factor of 6.3 in unsorted HHSC (p=0.0204, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from qPCR experiments on lentivirally transduced cells.

claim: Overexpression of GREM1 did not significantly affect the expression of COL1A1, ACTA2, or TIMP1 in either LX-2 or primary HHSC.
source: Overexpression did not significantly affect the expression of COL1A1, ACTA2, or TIMP1 in either LX-2 or primary HHSC (all p>0.05, Figure 4C and D).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from qPCR experiments on lentivirally transduced cells.

claim: GREM1 overexpression significantly increased the expression of LOX in vehicle control-treated LX-2 cells only (p=0.020).
source: However, in LX-2 cells, GREM1 overexpression significantly increased the expression LOX in vehicle control-treated cells only (p=0.020, Figure 4D), while CCL2 and LOXL1 expression were unaffected (p=0.11 and p=0.15, respectively).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from qPCR experiments on lentivirally transduced LX-2 cells.

claim: GREM1 overexpression did not affect CCL2 and LOXL1 expression in LX-2 cells (p=0.11 and p=0.15, respectively).
source: However, in LX-2 cells, GREM1 overexpression significantly increased the expression LOX in vehicle control-treated cells only (p=0.020, Figure 4D), while CCL2 and LOXL1 expression were unaffected (p=0.11 and p=0.15, respectively).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from qPCR experiments on lentivirally transduced LX-2 cells.

claim: GREM1 overexpression reduced BMP4, SMAD6, and SMAD7 expression in vehicle-treated LX-2 cells only (p=0.016, p=0.013, and p=0.032, respectively).
source: Moreover, GREM1 overexpression affected gene expression of several BMP-related signalling targets; BMP4, SMAD6, and SMAD7 expression were reduced in vehicle-treated cells only (p=0.016, p=0.013, and p=0.032, respectively, Figure 4E).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from qPCR experiments on lentivirally transduced LX-2 cells.

claim: GREM1 overexpression resulted in a significant downregulation of INHBB expression irrespective of TGFβ1 co-treatment (p=2.4 × 10–5).
source: Furthermore, GREM1 overexpression resulted in a significant downregulation of INHBB expression irrespective of TGFβ1 co-treatment (p=2.4 × 10–5) and upregulation of BMP7 and SMAD1 (p=0.008 and p=0.007, respectively, Figure 4E).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from qPCR experiments on lentivirally transduced LX-2 cells.

claim: GREM1 overexpression resulted in upregulation of BMP7 and SMAD1 (p=0.008 and p=0.007, respectively).
source: Furthermore, GREM1 overexpression resulted in a significant downregulation of INHBB expression irrespective of TGFβ1 co-treatment (p=2.4 × 10–5) and upregulation of BMP7 and SMAD1 (p=0.008 and p=0.007, respectively, Figure 4E).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from qPCR experiments on lentivirally transduced LX-2 cells.

claim: CDAA-HFD led to a reduction in body weight in rats.
source: As expected, CDAA-HFD led to a reduction in body weight and induced a MASH phenotype, as evidenced by increased plasma levels of alanine and aspartate aminotransferase (ALT and AST, respectively), increased liver weight, steatosis, picrosirius red (PSR) positive fibrosis area, and CD45+ immune cell infiltrates (Figure 5B–H).
evidence: Direct observation from in vivo rat experiments.

claim: CDAA-HFD induced a MASH phenotype in rats, as evidenced by increased plasma levels of ALT and AST, increased liver weight, steatosis, PSR positive fibrosis area, and CD45+ immune cell infiltrates.
source: As expected, CDAA-HFD led to a reduction in body weight and induced a MASH phenotype, as evidenced by increased plasma levels of alanine and aspartate aminotransferase (ALT and AST, respectively), increased liver weight, steatosis, picrosirius red (PSR) positive fibrosis area, and CD45+ immune cell infiltrates (Figure 5B–H).
evidence: Direct observation from in vivo rat experiments with multiple measured parameters.

claim: Gremlin-1 concentration increased with heparin-displacing antibody treatment in rats.
source: We did not find any Gremlin-1 protein in rats treated with isotype controls or non-heparin-displacing antibodies, but Gremlin-1 concentration increased with heparin-displacing antibody treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Gremlin-1 was removed from extracellular matrix and entered circulation.
evidence: Direct observation from AlphaLISA measurements on rat plasma samples.

claim: Gremlin-1 was removed from extracellular matrix and entered circulation upon heparin-displacing antibody treatment in rats.
source: We did not find any Gremlin-1 protein in rats treated with isotype controls or non-heparin-displacing antibodies, but Gremlin-1 concentration increased with heparin-displacing antibody treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Gremlin-1 was removed from extracellular matrix and entered circulation.
evidence: Inference based on increased circulating Gremlin-1 levels after heparin-displacing antibody treatment.

claim: Treatment with neither the heparin-displacing or non-displacing antibody changed MASH phenotype in rats, as measured by serum ALT or AST, liver weight, steatosis, PSR-positive area, or CD45+ cell infiltrate.
source: However, treatment with neither the heparin-displacing or non-displacing antibody did change MASH phenotype, as measured by serum ALT or AST, liver weight, steatosis, PSR-positive area, or CD45+ cell infiltrate (all p>0.05, Figure 5C–H).
evidence: Quantitative measurements from in vivo rat experiments showing no significant differences.

claim: Albumin concentrations and AST activity in PCLS supernatants were similar between treatment groups, indicating no toxicity of any of the compounds.
source: Albumin concentrations and AST activity in supernatants were similar between treatment groups, indicating no toxicity of any of the compounds (p=0.358 and p=0.112, respectively, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Quantitative measurements from PCLS experiments showing no significant differences in toxicity markers.

claim: Treatment with TGFβ1 increased the expression of COL1A1, ACTA2, and TIMP1 in PCLS (p=0.033, p=0.095, and p=0.047, respectively).
source: Treatment with TGFβ1 increased the expression of COL1A1, ACTA2, and TIMP1 (p=0.033, p=0.095, and p=0.047, respectively, Figure 6B), while ALK5 inhibition significantly decreased their expression (p=9.9 × 10–4, p=0.040, and p=0.003, respectively, Figure 6B).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from qPCR experiments on human PCLS.

claim: ALK5 inhibition significantly decreased the expression of COL1A1, ACTA2, and TIMP1 in PCLS (p=9.9 × 10–4, p=0.040, and p=0.003, respectively).
source: Treatment with TGFβ1 increased the expression of COL1A1, ACTA2, and TIMP1 (p=0.033, p=0.095, and p=0.047, respectively, Figure 6B), while ALK5 inhibition significantly decreased their expression (p=9.9 × 10–4, p=0.040, and p=0.003, respectively, Figure 6B).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from qPCR experiments on human PCLS.

claim: The anti-Gremlin-1 antibody did not reduce fibrotic marker expression when compared to the isotype control antibody in PCLS (p>0.283 in all comparisons).
source: The anti-Gremlin-1 antibody did not reduce fibrotic marker expression when compared to the isotype control antibody (p>0.283 in all comparisons, Figure 6B).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from qPCR experiments on human PCLS.

claim: No changes in soluble Pro-collagen 1A1 levels in PCLS supernatant were observed upon treatment with the anti-Gremlin-1 antibody.
source: Concordant with gene expression data, we also saw no changes in soluble Pro-collagen 1A1 levels in PCLS supernatant upon treatment with the anti-Gremlin-1 antibody (Figure 6C).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from protein assays on PCLS supernatants.

claim: The authors were unable to detect Gremlin-1 protein in PCLS supernatants.
source: Like for the target engagement studies in the rat CDAA-HFD model, we measured Gremlin-1 protein in PCLS supernatants but were unable to pick up any signal (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Direct observation from AlphaLISA measurements on PCLS supernatants.

claim: AF488-conjugated non-heparin-displacing antibody bound to scar tissue in PCLS, suggesting adequate tissue penetration.
source: However, using confocal microscopy on PCLS stained with AF488-conjugated non-heparin-displacing antibody, we observed binding of the therapeutic antibody but not the isotype control to scar tissue in PCLS, suggesting adequate tissue penetration (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Direct observation from confocal microscopy experiments on PCLS.

claim: Differential gene expression analysis did not show any considerable gene expression changes in response to anti-Gremlin-1 treatment in PCLS.
source: To check whether anti-Gremlin-1 treatment affected other pathways, we performed 3'-mRNA-sequencing on antibody-treated PCLS, but differential gene expression analysis did not show any considerable gene expression changes in response to anti-Gremlin-1 treatment (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: Analysis of 3'-mRNA-sequencing data from PCLS experiments.

claim: Gremlin-1 is a protein that is mainly expressed in fibroblasts and stem cells.
source: Gremlin-1 is a protein that is mainly expressed in fibroblasts and stem cells, and has been linked to fibrosis in a number of organs, including the kidney, lung, pancreas, and skin (Church et al., 2017; Koli et al., 2006; Staloch et al., 2015; Duffy et al., 2021).
evidence: Reference to published literature by Church et al., 2017; Koli et al., 2006; Staloch et al., 2015; Duffy et al., 2021.

claim: Gremlin-1 has been linked to fibrosis in the kidney, lung, pancreas, and skin.
source: Gremlin-1 is a protein that is mainly expressed in fibroblasts and stem cells, and has been linked to fibrosis in a number of organs, including the kidney, lung, pancreas, and skin (Church et al., 2017; Koli et al., 2006; Staloch et al., 2015; Duffy et al., 2021).
evidence: Reference to published literature by Church et al., 2017; Koli et al., 2006; Staloch et al., 2015; Duffy et al., 2021.

claim: Gremlin-1 acts mainly via inhibition of bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signalling by direct binding and inactivation of BMPs 2, 4, and 7.
source: It acts mainly via inhibition of bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signalling by direct binding and inactivation of BMPs 2, 4, and 7 (Topol et al., 2000), whilst some have reported actions on vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 and monocyte migration inhibitory factor (Mitola et al., 2010; Mueller et al., 2013).
evidence: Reference to published literature by Topol et al., 2000.

claim: Some have reported Gremlin-1 actions on vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 and monocyte migration inhibitory factor.
source: It acts mainly via inhibition of bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signalling by direct binding and inactivation of BMPs 2, 4, and 7 (Topol et al., 2000), whilst some have reported actions on vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 and monocyte migration inhibitory factor (Mitola et al., 2010; Mueller et al., 2013).
evidence: Reference to published literature by Mitola et al., 2010; Mueller et al., 2013.

claim: Gremlin-1 forms dimers and avidly binds to glycosaminoglycans such as heparin and heparan sulphate.
source: Gremlin-1 forms dimers and avidly binds to glycosaminoglycans such as heparin and heparan sulphate, although the latter is not necessary for its interaction with BMPs (Grillo et al., 2016; Tatsinkam et al., 2017; Kišonaitė et al., 2016; Tatsinkam et al., 2015).
evidence: Reference to published literature by Grillo et al., 2016; Tatsinkam et al., 2017; Kišonaitė et al., 2016; Tatsinkam et al., 2015.

claim: Heparan sulphate binding is not necessary for Gremlin-1's interaction with BMPs.
source: Gremlin-1 forms dimers and avidly binds to glycosaminoglycans such as heparin and heparan sulphate, although the latter is not necessary for its interaction with BMPs (Grillo et al., 2016; Tatsinkam et al., 2017; Kišonaitė et al., 2016; Tatsinkam et al., 2015).
evidence: Reference to published literature by Grillo et al., 2016; Tatsinkam et al., 2017; Kišonaitė et al., 2016; Tatsinkam et al., 2015.

claim: In the liver, Gremlin-1 expression is generally low and restricted to activated hepatic stellate cells (HSC).
source: In the liver, expression is generally low (Gustafson et al., 2015) and restricted to activated hepatic stellate cells (HSC), which are the main fibrogenic cell population in the liver along with fibroblasts (Boers et al., 2006; Ogawa et al., 2007).
evidence: Reference to published literature by Gustafson et al., 2015; Boers et al., 2006; Ogawa et al., 2007.

claim: Activated hepatic stellate cells (HSC) are the main fibrogenic cell population in the liver along with fibroblasts.
source: In the liver, expression is generally low (Gustafson et al., 2015) and restricted to activated hepatic stellate cells (HSC), which are the main fibrogenic cell population in the liver along with fibroblasts (Boers et al., 2006; Ogawa et al., 2007).
evidence: Reference to published literature by Boers et al., 2006; Ogawa et al., 2007.

claim: Hepatic Gremlin-1 has been linked to hepatocellular insulin resistance.
source: Hepatic Gremlin-1 has been linked to hepatocellular insulin resistance (Hedjazifar et al., 2020) and recent literature described a role in driving hepatocellular senescence, which in turn is linked to hepatic fibrogenesis and carcinogenesis (Baboota et al., 2022).
evidence: Reference to published literature by Hedjazifar et al., 2020.

claim: Gremlin-1 has a role in driving hepatocellular senescence, which in turn is linked to hepatic fibrogenesis and carcinogenesis.
